## The note underneath decides what the chord is

Whatever sits lowest changes how you hear everything above it. Put the root on
every downbeat and the progression becomes trivially easy to identify, which is
useful for about eight bars and then starts to feel like a spreadsheet. A bass
line gets direction when you treat those roots as destinations and connect them:
chord tones, passing tones, and *approach notes*, pitches a semitone above or
below the next target.

Start with bare roots anyway, because they give you a reference. If your
progression doesn't state itself clearly with four long roots, adding motion
will hide the fault, not fix it. Once the roots work, keep their downbeat
arrivals fixed and change only the route between them. Now the comparison tells
you exactly what the connective notes contribute.

Rhythm is the other half. A bass sustains a downbeat, walks in quarter notes, or
arrives at the next root early, off the beat. Its pattern answers the harmony
without copying the melody's durations, and that's what turns the bottom of a
chord into a part you can follow.

## Four roots, then four routes

The progression runs C, A minor, F, G. First you'll hear the four roots alone,
one per bar. Then the walking version fills each bar with quarter notes: root,
fifth, a directional passing tone, and a chromatic approach from below into the
next downbeat. Both passes reach the same four roots at the same four moments,
so what is the second one actually adding?

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92
use_synth :fm

roots = [note(:c2), note(:a1), note(:f1), note(:g1)]

define :play_root_bass do |root_notes|
  root_notes.each do |root|
    play root, release: 3.6, amp: 0.7
    sleep 4
  end
end

define :play_walking_bass do |root_notes|
  root_notes.each_with_index do |root, index|
    next_root = root_notes[(index + 1) % root_notes.length]
    fifth = root + 7
    passing = root + (next_root > root ? 4 : -3)
    approach = next_root - 1

    [root, fifth, passing, approach].each do |pitch|
      play pitch, release: 0.75, amp: 0.7
      sleep 1
    end
  end
end

play_root_bass roots
sleep 2
play_walking_bass roots
```

Four pillars in the first statement. In the second, those pillars stay exactly
where they were, but by beat 4 the bass is already leaning into the next one.
Listen to the semitone between each approach note and the root that follows it.
That single half-step is what makes the arrival sound intended.

## Reroute the walk

1. Change `approach` to `next_root + 1` so every chromatic note falls into its
   target from above. Compare the approach into all four roots. One formula
   won't give you equally convincing voice leading at every boundary.
2. Restore the approach and set `fifth` to `root + 12`. An octave reinforces the
   root and adds no new chord tone. The line gets wider, and its second beat now
   repeats an identity you already had.
3. Zip the four pitches with durations `[1.5, 0.5, 1, 1]`. The bar still totals
   four beats. A held opening root followed by a quick second event changes the
   gait completely, and against a melody in steady quarter notes you'll hear the
   two parts stop marching in step.

## What the approach note buys you

Low register carries unusual perceptual weight, which is why downbeat roots
define the sequence on their own. Everything between them can be unstable for a
moment, so long as the structural targets land clearly and on time. A chromatic
approach sits outside the current chord, and its half-step resolution explains
its presence the instant it arrives.

Passing tones need somewhere to go. Two roots a third apart leave room for a
single scale step with obvious direction. Across a wider interval, put chord
tones on strong beats and the less stable pitches in weak metrical positions.
These constraints interact; they aren't a lookup table of permitted notes. Next
root, current chord, meter and melodic register all pull on the same choice.

The four roots stay as source data and one function derives everything else,
which leaves the root-only bass sitting there as a regression test. If your
walking version lands on the wrong downbeat, check the indexing and the duration
sum before you start replacing pitches. Harmony and timeline fail
independently.

Down here, timbre changes too. A pitch that stays articulate on a piano turns to
undifferentiated rumble on an FM or sub-bass synth, because its partials stack
up differently through speakers than through headphones. Try the whole line an
octave higher before you reach for the amp. Turning down a muddy line leaves the
mud exactly where it was.

## Walk an eight-bar progression

Take an eight-bar progression from an earlier harmony lesson. Render one root
per bar first. Then derive a walking line that hits those same roots on every
downbeat, with at least four chromatic approaches and four diatonic passing
tones, each named in a comment so you can review your own reasoning later.

Give the walking line a rhythm your melody doesn't have, and validate every
bar's total. Play the root version and the walking version back to back. You're
listening for one thing: whether the added motion clarifies the route between
chords, or whether it has quietly weakened the arrivals it was supposed to
prepare.
